summary:
Bayelsa State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework on sexual orientation and gender identity, with no state-specific enforcement divergence documented for it. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across Nigeria since 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. The statute renders any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void, bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and reaches participants and guests at same-sex weddings, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.

The maximum penalty for same-sex sexual activity in Bayelsa is 14 years' imprisonment. The death penalty is confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where penalties range from lashes or caning up to death by stoning; a Shari'a court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and a further death-by-stoning sentence from Bauchi was reported in May 2024. In January 2014 a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial. Bayelsa, in the southern portion of the country, stands under the secular national 14-year framework and does not face Shari'a-based death-penalty risk.

Nigeria offers no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct federally, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in some northern states.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Bayelsa's position in southern Nigeria places it under the secular national penal framework rather than the Shari'a codes operating in the twelve northern states, which is the sharpest legal divide affecting LGBT+ travellers in Nigeria. The northern death-penalty risk documented in Bauchi and elsewhere does not apply in Bayelsa, though the 14-year maximum for same-sex conduct does.

The national pattern of police extortion and arbitrary arrest documented in Lagos and Abuja is reported as countrywide by the UK Home Office, suggesting that Bayelsa visitors should expect similar exposure to pretextual stops even without a state-specific incident on record.

Nigeria's lack of legal gender recognition means a trans visitor's documents will likely present a gender marker inconsistent with presentation, which interacts with the criminal exposure around cross-dressing proposals and with police discretion at stops.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have since been enacted is unresolved in the sources available here.

No Bayelsa-specific enforcement incidents, arrests, or prosecutions of trans or gender-nonconforming people are documented in this inventory; the state-level picture rests on the national framework with no recorded divergence, which is an absence of evidence rather than evidence of non-enforcement.
